Madam Speaker, I thank you for your assistance.
Some of those people who are watching may be surprised to know that the piece of legislation before the House is an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and that it has to do with sales taxes. I just want to mention a few of the things with which these increased taxes have to do.
There is a 10 per cent tax on telecommunication services, telephones, telex services. There is an increase in the telecommunications programming tax on cable and pay-television services. There is an increase in the sales tax on paint and wallpaper products. There is an acceleration of federal sales tax and excise tax remittances. There is an increase in the federal sales tax on beer, spirits, wines, and tobacco. The list goes on and on.
These increased taxes did not come about as an act of God. They came from a series of Budgets that the Conservative Government imposed upon Canadians. The Acts that we are
dealing with today concern the Minister of Finance's Budgets of February 18, 1987 and February 10, 1988; his June 18, 1987 White Paper on tax reform, and his December 16, 1987 tax reform paper.
What we have here are a series of tax increases coming out of papers that the Government called "tax reform". In a nutshell, that is what this debate is about. It is the Mulroney Conservative Government imposing tax increases upon Canadians in the name of tax reform. In the next few months, by sleight of hand, the Conservatives hope to create the opposite impression from what they have in fact been doing. We all know that in July people will be receiving some small measure of tax relief. When one looks at the over-all balance of things and takes into account all of the increases in tax burden that the Conservative Government has laid upon the backs of ordinary Canadians, the tax relief that will be delivered this summer is but a fraction of the tax increase. The over-all balance will mean tax increases.
In sum, Madam Speaker, tax reform to Tories spells tax increases. As a result of the Conservative Budgets over the last few years the average family is facing an increase in tax burden of $1,500. This might be justifiable if everybody else had been required to bear the same burden, or the money was being spent so wisely that it was evident to every Canadian that a tax increase was necessary.
Let us look at the first aspect of that proposition. Is everybody else carrying their fair share of the burden? What about corporations? What about large, profitable, powerful multinational corporations in Canada that make millions of dollars in profits and end up paying no taxes? In 1987, Xerox Canada made millions of dollars of profits and paid no taxes. The same holds true for a whole series of large and profitable corporations. Not only did those corporations pay no taxes and therefore set the tax burden that ordinary Canadian families have faced as a result of Tory policy in an unfair context, but many of those corporations received tax credits. They received dollars from the taxes of ordinary Canadians. In some cases, large corporations which made hundreds of millions of dollars in profits received tens of millions of dollars in tax credits as gifts from the Conservative Government of the day.
I do not wish to be overly partisan and say that this idea was originated by the Conservative Party, because I am aware of the fact that this trend was started under previous Liberal Governments. This policy of going easy on profitable corporations and going tough on ordinary Canadian families was started by the Liberals.
When Canadians voted for change in the last election, it is unfortunate that they did not receive real change. They did not get a government that was going to bring about real tax reform. Instead, they got the same old Liberal policies under a new partisan label. They got tax reform that translated into tax increases.

Pass it and we will get some tax reform.
May 26, 1988

How can the Conservatives justify the fact that they have increased the tax burden on the ordinary family by some $1,500 over the last three years? Have they asked everyone in the country to pay their fair share? Clearly they have not had the courage, the will, or the intention to ask corporations to do that, not just any corporation, but profitable corporations. What about wealthy individuals? There are people in this country who make more than $50,000 and $100,000 in personal income and who, because of tax writeoffs pay no taxes.
During the last federal election the then candidate for Prime Minister, now Prime Minister, (Mr. Mulroney), promised a minimum income tax, after he was prodded in that direction by the Leader of our Party who was calling for real tax reform. In the televised leadership debate the now Prime Minister then stated that he would bring about a minimum income tax. Once he got into office he moved as slow as a snail, as quick as a turtle, and eventually did bring forward some form of minimum income tax. At that time we welcomed the fact that he was taking action. But we also wanted to take some time to see whether or not this tax was going to bear fruit.
What studies and commentators have found is that the minimum income tax on wealthy individuals introduced by the Conservative Party is having a marginal impact. Because of exemptions, many of those wealthy individuals continue to pay no taxes. How can the Conservatives ask the ordinary Canadian family to pay more taxes, while many wealthy individuals who earn $50,000 or $100,000 pay no taxes? The whole question of taxation is one that leaves the ordinary Canadian with a sense of unfairness, that they are being asked to pay more while others are getting a free ride.
I would like to address the matter of tax reform and this matter of the continual pattern of tax increases by the Conservative Government from another perspective, that is, from the perspective of revenues, and what revenues could be collected if we asked those people who are getting a free ride now to pay taxes.
For example, in his annual report the Auditor General has identified $30 billion to $40 billion of tax write-offs which he says are questionable; there are serious questions about whether or not these tax expenditures achieve the public purpose objectives for which they were put in place. I am referring for example, to incentives for investment to create growth and employment. The Auditor General, who is an objective officer of Parliament, has stated that these tax writeoffs do not achieve the objectives for which they have been established. Those are tax expenditures, forgiven taxes in order to achieve certain objectives, and the Auditor General says we do not know whether those objectives are being achieved and there is no basis upon which we can confidently say that they are being achieved.
Excise Tax Act
We are giving up revenues. Instead of giving up those revenues for questionable purposes and collecting them we could provide some tax relief for the ordinary families. I want to assure you, Madam Speaker, that, based on my experience of talking to hundreds of citizens in my own riding of Winnipeg North Centre, the average family today is feeling the burden of taxation. People are fed up with this burden and they are angry that they are continually being asked to pay more and more and more. We allow these tax expenditures of $30 billion or $40 billion to leak through the tax system sieve. If we collected those revenues, a portion of them would provide the money for some tax relief for ordinary families who would not have to face such a heavy burden of taxation.
Now, $30 billion or $40 billion is a significant amount of money. Not only could we provide tax relief with it but we could also use it to attack some of the most glaring social problems in society. Canadians are compassionate. We have a sense of justice and a sense of fairness. It is shocking that we have people who are homeless and that there are children who do not have a roof over their heads. Some families do not have enough to eat. There are extremely acute social problems which could be attacked if we collected the tax revenues which are now being expended in a questionable way, according to the Auditor General. What about the tax increases which the Conservatives have brought about? We ought to look at revenues which the Conservatives are allowing to slip away. People who are getting a free ride in our society, the powerful and the wealthy, should pay their fair share, then we could give some relief to the ordinary family and take action on some very acute problems such as those of the homeless and hungry.
I want to approach this question of Tory tax increases, so-called tax reform, from another perspective. What are our priorities for the revenues once we collect them? If we are increasing taxes, the Government must have a purpose for the money which is being taken out of the pockets of ordinary Canadian families.
This Government has embarked on a program of having nuclear submarines. Estimates of the cost of this program are in the neighbourhood of $8 billion. When I consider that, I have serious questions about the Government's judgment that it has to increase the taxes for ordinary Canadian families. Is the reason for increasing taxes that the Conservatives want to play this macho game of nuclear submarines, spending billions of dollars to purchase them so they can play in the big leagues with the Americans and Soviets? Could they not find an effective, more modest and realistic way of achieving the security objectives of Canada without wasting the money of hard pressed families on the purchase of nuclear submarines?
It is ironic that we are embarking on the possibility of purchasing very expensive subs from France, for example, a country which is giving us such a hard time with the fishery in Atlantic Canada. Why are we offering to give billions of dollars to a country that says it does not care what happens to

May 26, 1988
Excise Tax Act
our inshore fishermen and does not care about negotiations because it is bigger, more powerful and more significant on the international stage than Canada? Why are we taxing ordinary Canadian families to give bushels of money to a country that is pushing us around when it comes to the fishery? Fundamentally I do not think the Government can justify the tax increase on ordinary Canadians by $ 1,500 over the last three years. I do not think the Government can justify that, given the priorities it has established on spending and given the fact that the Government wants to use so much of this money to purchase nuclear submarines. I believe the majority of Canadians would reject this nuclear program out of hand. It is a program about which Canadians have not been consulted in any effective way. If they were, I am sure they would say no to it. The Government is wasting money when it comes to expenditures. Money could be saved and the Government could take a more modest and yet effective approach to them.
The Government is allowing revenues to go uncollected. The Government is allowing a whole series of tax write-offs to continue to exist for which there is no documentation. Billions of dollars of revenues are flowing away. A recent study was done by an economist from, I believe, Newfoundland in which he indicated that for every dollar of tax revenue that is given up only 21 cents of new investment is generated. That raises the question of the effectiveness of tax write-offs when only 21 cents of investment is generated each time a dollar is spent. That does not sound like a very economical approach to me because every time you go down that road you lose money.
The legislation before the House today to amend the Excise Tax Act is a series of tax increases. It is from a number of Budgets, a couple of which have been called tax reform papers, but when it comes down to it what tax reform means to Tories is tax increases. The burden on the ordinary Canadian family has increased over the last few years since the Conservative Government has taken office and this legislation is implementing that policy. There is no way you can justify tax increases without first indicating that everyone is paying his or her fair share. We know that profitable corporations in Canada are getting away with paying no taxes. Corporations that make profits and pay no taxes end up getting tax credits and are walking away with the money of ordinary Canadian families. That is unfair. It has to stop and the way to do it is to throw those chaps on that side of the House out of office. That will happen in short order, just as soon as the Prime Minister gets up enough courage to call the next election.
I wish that the Conservative Government would own up to the fact that when it says tax reform, it means tax increases. At least then it would have the virtue of honesty and frankness. It should back away from the policy and give some tax relief to ordinary Canadian families.

Madam Speaker, it is true that the NDP did vote against the National Energy Program, but I would refer my hon. friend to House of Commons Debates of October 23, 1981, when the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) who was the energy critic for the NDP said:
Today I want to begin the debate on the Canadianization parts of Bill C-48. These clauses of the bill lie at the heart of the National Energy Program. They are the ones under a barrage of unparalleled criticism from our American friends.
1 want to tell the government on behalf of our party, and indirectly the United States government, that the objectives of the National Energy Program will get our support, and I think public support, provided the legislation is tightened up to fully reflect that...
I regret to say there has been evidence in the last few days that the Canadian government is backing off the National Energy Program and its objectives under American pressure.
It is obvious that although the NDP did vote against the National Energy Program, it was not because NDP Members disagreed with it but because the Liberal Government, they said, was not going far enough. How does he square that or what does he mean by that?

Madam Speaker, I am glad that my hon. colleague acknowledged the fact that this Party voted against the National Energy Program. After he did that, my hon. colleague engaged in a time-honoured parliamentary ploy which is to take a speech from many years ago, find a quote and seek to embarrass someone. We see that going on in the House every day. Someone on this side reads a statement of a Minister on that side made when he or she was in Opposition, someone on that side reads what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) said when he was in such and such a position. This goes on all the time.
While the Hoti. Member is engaging in this game, I will point out one thing about the quote that he read to me, and that is, that the quote was qualified. There was a specific reference to the phrase "provided that". Obviously when my hon. colleague was speaking at that time, there were some conditions attached to what he was saying. I do not claim to
May 26, 1988

know the contents of all of the speeches of all of my colleagues back throughout history.
I would like my hon. friend across the way to deal with the fact that his Government has increased the tax burden on ordinary Canadians over the last three years by some $1,500. How could he do that at the same time that he allows profitable corporations to get away with paying no taxes whatsoever?

Madam Speaker, while one cannot expect the Hon. Member to remember all the speeches given by his colleagues, surely Canadians should be able to expect that members of the NDP remain consistent in every regard with regard to their national policy. I do not want to get into another battle with members of the NDP and their inconsistencies and hypocrisies. 1 want to ask the Hon. Member a question.
I listened to the Hon. Member's speech very carefully. I wonder if he could comment on the smoke and mirrors used by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the accounting trickery used by the Conservative Government with regard to the deficit. The Government likes to boast about the fact that the deficit has decreased over the last several years, but I am sure the Hon. Member will agree with me when I say that, to a large extent, it is all smoke and mirrors. It has all been done very surreptitiously, using accounting tricks.
One such trick is the acceleration of employer remittances. As the Hon. Member knows, up until this pseudo-Government came to office, employers were required to remit income tax, UIC and CPP payments once a month. As a result of an accounting trick and in order to reduce the deficit by over $1 billion, the Government has required employers to make those remittances, first, every two weeks and, I understand, now weekly, to give the impression that the deficit has been reduced when in fact it is all tricks and smoke and mirrors. The deficit really is not reduced by the figure $1.6 billion; it is just reduced for a period of a week or two weeks in order to make the Minister of Finance look good. In so doing, the Government is affecting the cash flow of many small businesses. I wonder if the Hon. Member has any thoughts on that.

Madam Speaker, I find it interesting that my hon. colleague from the Liberal Party applies a moral standard to the NDP that of course no one would even try to apply to the Liberal Party, and that is consistency. If there is any Canadian who believes that Liberals hold consistency to be the highest principle, then I will seek to answer the question the Hon. Member asked about consistency.
Clearly the Government is engaged in smoke and mirrors with the deficit, but it is also engaged in something else. It is pursuing a policy that was started by the previous Liberal Government, in particular a policy that was started by the Hon. Member who is now the Leader of the Liberal Party (Mr. Turner), and that is the policy of giving a free ride to profitable corporations.

If the Conservative Government and the previous Liberal Government had required profitable corporations to pay taxes, then there would be revenues so that the books could be balanced. There would be a way to reduce the deficit significantly and at the same time provide tax relief for ordinary Canadian families.

Madam Speaker, I am most happy to be able to speak to this issue. I cannot believe the statements coming from the mouths of NDP Members in the House of Commons today. We hear the Hon. Member talking about tax burdens and corporate tax rip-offs. When members of the NDP saw the effectiveness of the flow-through shares that were introduced by the previous Liberal Government, that so-called tax loophole, they did a quicker flip-flop on that issue than we have seen in a very long time. They do not mind standing up and preaching "no tax loopholes" except when it is a tax loophole that happens to be working.
That makes sense.

We do not mind people on either side of the House saying they are going to close off all tax loopholes, but please do not try to have it both ways. The NDP House Leader was actually wearing a button which said "save the flow" at the same time as the NDP finance critic was standing up in the House blasting away at corporate tax exemptions.
What hypocrisy.

I think the NDP owes this House an explanation. I hope for goodness' sake that when they talk about consistency they do not follow the pattern of their socialist colleagues in New Zealand who were the first in the western world to impose a tax on food. The socialist Government of New Zealand imposed a tax on food, and that was defended in this House. I am glad the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) is here because he will recall that when I asked him whether his Party, if it were the Government, would follow the example of the Government of New Zealand, he defended that socialist Government and its imposition of a tax on food.
I did not defend the tax on food and would not do it now.

As a matter of fact, if the Hon. Member with thin skin will look it up in Hansard, he will find that I asked him what he thought of this move by the socialist Government of New Zealand. He thought that Government had its own political agenda, and he was not prepared to criticize, God forbid, that socialist Government.
That is not what we are dealing with in this legislation but I think it has to be dealt with in the over-all context of tax reform because it is very easy for the NDP to stand up and rail

May 26, 1988
Excise Tax Act
away at what past Liberal Governments have done and the general tax propositions of the current Government. However, it is also transparently obvious to taxpayers that the NDP wants to have it both ways. They cannot because they have to be consistent in their tax policy.
Also on the question of consistency, there is one inconsistent spokesperson for the Government whose public statements boggle the mind. I refer to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). On November 29, 1984, he said that Canadians pay a good deal of money for government services and feel they are already paying quite enough. Both he and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) campaigned on a promise that they would not raise taxes. Here is a direct quote from the Minister of Finance on March 6, 1984: "We will reduce spending. We will refrain from increasing taxes which are already too high." Instead, we have a Government which has increased taxes in probably the largest amount of any government in the history of Canada.
In January, 1988, the Government imposed a 10 per cent tax on telecommunication services, that is, the telephone. We have already heard the very articulate Member for Glengarry-Prescott

Russell (Mr. Boudria) point out how inconsistent that tax measure is because it penalizes in particular those Canadians who must, by virtue of where they live, use longdistance to communicate with family, friends, doctors and others. It is basically their lifeline to the community. Yet the Government implements a 10 per cent tax on telecommunication services.
We had an increase on tax on telecommunication programming services; an increase in the sales tax on paint and wallpaper products, and acceleration of federal sales and excise tax remittances, a scam which was just referred to by my colleague, the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata).
The Minister of Finance stands in his place and says the Government is paying down the deficit. What it is doing is robbing the cash flow of small Canadian companies already living on the edge, scratching by their fingernails for mere existence. Instead of being able to collect their receivables and pay their payables, in many cases they have to pay the Government before they even receive it themselves. This accelerated payment is actually costing hundreds of millions of dollars in lost cash flow for small Canadian businesses, which are the life-blood of this country. It is not the large corporations which have created jobs in the 1980s. It has been the small businesses, in particular those started by women. Those businesses are being gouged by a Minister of Finance who claims he is paying down the deficit when in fact he is merely speeding up the collection process which robs the cash flow which is so crucial to the life of many small businesses.
We also see further increases in excise taxes on tobacco products, beer, spirits and wine. There is an air transportation levy. That tax discriminates against northerners and those who, by virtue of their distance from major centres, have to use
air transportation to visit hospitals or doctors. There is an increase in the excise tax on gasoline and aviation fuel.
The amount of money the Government has raised in tax measures over its years in office is unbelievable. There has been a 46 per cent tax increase from 1984 to 1989. If you take into account personal income tax increases amounting to 55 per cent, a 77 per cent increase in sales and excise taxes which the Minister stated were job killers, and an increase of 16 per cent in other taxes, the total increase is 46 per cent from a Government which promised no tax increases.
Who is paying these taxes? Is it wealthy Canadians who are in the best position to pay? My Leader pointed out only a few days ago in the House that the only group who seemed to be getting a break by way of a reduction in tax burden are those earning over $100,000 a year. The Minister of Finance wants to slap a tax on people earning $15,000 a year and less, but he does not mind giving out $500,000 in capital gains exemptions. That was reduced finally to $100,000 in the last Budget, but it is an indication of government priorities. He is prepared to tell a single parent earning $15,000 a year that he or she should pay taxes, yet if you happen to be in the top 2 per cent of income earners you can have a $500,000 capital gains exemption. Most people in my riding do not even know what a capital gain is. Yet the top 2 per cent are getting a $500,000 tax write-off from a Government which claims it is not going to increase taxes. Well, it did not increase taxes for that group, but for most Canadians the effect of the Government's tax policies has been a double whammy.
The 77 per cent increase in sales and excise taxes in particular is damaging to those with low and moderate incomes. That is obvious. If I happen to be earning $70,000 a year and a waitress in my community happens to be earning $17,000 a year and we both decide to wallpaper our living room, the cost in excess taxes to that person is going to be the same as it is for me. Is that fair?
I submit that when the Minister of Finance said that sales and excise taxes were the silent killers of jobs, he was in fact speaking the truth and that, unfortunately, in his quest to help wealthy Canadians get richer by applying the capital gains exemptions, in his quest to show on paper that he is reducing the deficit, he has decided to penalize Canadians who are in the weakest position to fight back, those being, in particular, low and middle-income Canadians.
Many people in my own riding who have just filed their income tax were shocked and have written to me. They did not realize that over the tenure of the Government, the last four years, the Government has been silently chipping away at their earning power. They were surprised and shocked, when the time came to pay their income tax, to find that their tax bill was up to $1500 more than what it had been under previous Liberal Governments.
May 26, 1988

Look at the tax grab of major tax increases for individuals introduced by the Conservative Government. It picked up $1 billion in 1984 with a 1 per cent increase in sales tax. That was the first whammy. It picked up another $1 billion with the second increase of 1 per cent in sales tax in 1986. A third increase in 1986 picked up another $1 billion.
A two cent a litre increase in gas resulted in $930 million in excess revenue to the Queen's coffers. The second increase on gas earned $450 million, and the third in 1987 earned $450 million, for a grand total of $1,830 billion in gas tax increases alone.
The equalization of sales tax on unleaded and leaded gasoline in 1987 resulted in an extra $30 million coming into the federal coffers. The kiddy tax on candies and soft drinks and the sales tax on pet food earned $400 million. The extension of sales tax on snack foods earned $60 million.
The first increase in cigarette and tobacco taxes earned $320 million. The second increase in the so-called sin taxes resulted in a $150 million increase in tobacco and alcohol taxes. The third increase in 1987 amounted to $70 million.
The elimination of the RHOSP has to take the cake. I congratulate the Member from Toronto who is decrying the cost of housing in Toronto and would like to see a Toronto based Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan launched. Where was the Member when, in the Government's first Budget, it eliminated the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan and the Liberal Party in Opposition demanded that the Government reinstate it? Where was he when the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation doubled the cost of guaranteeing the purchase of a home, which effectively added $800 to the price of a new home anywhere in Canada?
Where was the voice from Toronto when the Government decided to pay down the deficit on paper on the backs of working Canadian men and women who are trying to be in a position to own their own homes?
Where was he when his own Finance Minister, from his beloved City of Toronto, the same city that does not warrant designation as a financial centre, increased the tax on building supplies and materials, which added a further $400 to $800 to the average cost of a home anywhere in Canada? The RHOSP would have potentially given tax breaks of $1,000 per year per person, $2,000 per year per family which, over 20 years, amounts to a tax break of $20,000.
Now that they are going to have some kind of international economic summit in Toronto the Member jumps on the bandwagon and claims to be fighting for working men and women in the City of Toronto when he sat in his seat silent for three and one-half years while the federal Government did everything it could to try to increase the cost to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation by eliminating the RHOSP, by increasing building supply materials, and by standing back and allowing the burden and responsibility for a
Excise Tax Act
national housing strategy to fall back on the shoulders of provincial Governments.
The elimination of RHOSP was another $105 million benefit to the federal coffers. The deindexation of the tax system earned $635 million. The elimination of the federal tax reduction amounted to another $650 million. Changes to marital exemptions saved the federal coffers $20 million. The general 3 per cent surtax of 1986 amounted to $1.2 million. The general temporary 5 per cent and 10 per cent surtaxes of 1986 amounted to another $500 million. The 10 per cent tax on long-distance calls of 1988 earned $945 million. Increases on other sales taxes amounted to $370 million. This list, long and complete though it may be, does not include the new federal sales tax imposed on June 18, 1987.
As soon as the Prime Minister got elected on a platform of no tax increases, on a platform of protection of senior citizens, on a platform of protection of universality, he immediately waged a campaign to increase taxes, to cut back on senior citizens' pensions and to damage and destroy universality.
Is it any wonder that the Canadian taxpayer is getting a little bit cynical about governments? Is it any wonder that when the Prime Minister stands up to give a speech, people ask themselves whether this man can be trusted to keep his word? He campaigned in 1984 on a simple promise that he was not going to increase taxes. Yet he has increased taxes more quickly and more unjustly than any Prime Minister since Confederation.

I do not believe, Madam Speaker, that Canadians can trust a Prime Minister who during the election campaign claimed that he hated tax increases, whether on personal income or on direct taxes like the sales tax, because we can see very clearly that even before the election, he was claiming that there would be no tax increases, but once he was elected, since his Government took power, we have had specific tax increases: a 55 per cent increase on personal income, a 28 per cent increase on corporate income, a 77 per cent increase of sales taxes, Madam Speaker, between 1984 and 1989, and a 16 per cent increase on other income, for a total average tax increase of 46 per cent; this from a Government that claims it does not want to increase taxes for Canadians.
Furthermore, Madam Speaker, we must consider the fact that the most affected, those who suffer most from tax increases are the least wealthy because, if one looks at the figures, the greatest tax increase is for the sales tax and the excise tax that we are now discussing; the poorest are the hardest hit. For example, someone who needs to buy something to repair his house pays the same tax, whether he is a millionaire or poor. That is why the Minister of Finance claimed that the sales tax kills jobs. Indeed it does. But why did the Government and the Prime Minister take office promising Canadians that they would not increase taxes? But since they have been in power, Canadians have had the biggest tax increases since Confederation. People are wondering, Madam

Speaker, and I think that Canadians will reject this Government once the Prime Minister has the courage to call an election.

Madam Speaker, I was fascinated by the Hon. Member's comments, particularly as they refer to myself. I was particularly interested because I was not aware that the Hon. Member even knew that I was in the House these days. However, I seem to have hit a nerve. As a result of that, I would like to pose a question or two to the Hon. Member.
The Hon. Member referred to a number of items in her comments. She knows that Canada faces a lot of problems, many of which were created by her Party when it formed the Government.
One of those problems in particular is the deficit. Many of the comments she made obviously referred to efforts of the Government to deal with the deficit, which would be approaching some $40 billion a year at the present time if action had not been taken by this Government. The deficit has been reduced by some $10 billion a year.
Does the Hon. Member and her Party want to see the national annual spending deficit of Canada reduced? If so, is it her position and the position of the Liberal Party that that deficit should not be reduced by raising taxes? Is she prepared to say now that the Liberal Party would not raise taxes if it formed the Government?
In conjunction with that, is she prepared to say specifically what expenditures would be cut back by the Liberal Party-if in fact it is interested in reducing the deficit-in order to reduce the deficit by $10 billion as it has been reduced on an annual basis in the last three and a half years?
Will the Hon. Member answer those questions? Does she and her Party support deficit reduction? If so, will she give us a commitment today that if and when her Party forms a government again in this country they will not raise taxes, unlike her provincial colleagues in Ontario where she served previously? Will she also tell us specifically what government expenditures would be cut by the Liberal Party in order to reduce the deficit by some $10 billion a year?
Madam Speaker, herein lies the difference between the Conservative and Liberal Parties. The Liberal Party is not prepared to make promises that it cannot keep.
Oh, oh!

During the 1984 election, the Leader of the Liberal Party, who has integrity and is accepted as an honest person across Canada, did not travel from St. John's, Newfoundland, to Chilliwack, British Columbia and tell people that he would keep taxes down and reduce the deficit at the same time.
The person who made that promise was the Leader of the Conservative Party. He tried to talk out of both sides of his mouth.
In fact, the Leader of the Liberal Party said quite bluntly that if the deficit is going to be reduced, he cannot make the promise that taxes will not be increased.
Consider the situation in the City of Toronto from the point of view of the Minister of Finance. The Government is telling Canadians that it is introducing fairness in tax measures. Yet for the first time it is slapping a tax on a single mother living in the Jane Finch area who is earning $15,000 a year. She is paying tax for the first time, while those wealthy enough to be in the top two per cent of the population and can accrue $500,000 in capital gains can get a tax holiday. Most of my constituents do not even know what a capital gain is.
The Government talks about tax fairness. Where is the fairness in a policy that offers a write-off to someone in the top 2 per cent of the population while telling a mother in the Jane Finch area that she must pay taxes?
The Member stood up in response to my direct challenge to him, but he did not answer my question. While I say, more power to the Member for calling for reintroduction of the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan just in advance of the economic summit, and only in the City of Toronto, where was he when the opposition Parties were in the trenches fighting the Government's decision to withdraw the RHOSP? Where was the Member when the Government doubled the guarantees that were forced on home owners who want to get CMHC insurance? The Government introduced successive Budgets in the interest of so-called deficit reduction, which did not translate into actual dollars. Where was the Member when the Government increased the sales tax on building materials that directly translates into increased cost of housing in Toronto?
The Hon. Member was standing on the sidelines, telling the Minister to go ahead and reduce the deficit on the backs of poor Canadians so that wealthy Canadians can get a half a million dollar capital gains write-off.
If the Member is serious about his intent to see a reintroduction of the RHOSP, he should throw off that Conservative yoke and join a real Party that will fight for working people, instead of the hypocrisy of the Conservative tax policy.

Madam Speaker, the Hon. member criticized the Conservative Government for the increase in taxes it has imposed on most Canadians. There are two groups of Canadians whose taxes have not been touched.
One group is that of wealthy individuals. There are over
5,000	wealthy Canadians who earned more than $50,000 last year and paid no income tax. There are 250 Canadians who had incomes of over $250,000 and paid no income tax. Is that not the same situation as existed in all the years the Liberals formed the Government?

We know that some of the largest corporations in Canada paid no corporation tax, including Alcan Aluminum, Brascan, Hees International, Power Financial, Xerox, Wardair and Union Carbide. They paid no corporation income tax in 1986 and in 1987, neither did the Hudson's Bay Company, Brama-lea and Cadillac-Fairview.

Why should Canadians believe the Liberal Party now when it criticizes the Conservatives for doing exactly what the Liberals did for so many years when they were in government?

Madam Speaker, I cannot believe what I am hearing. The Member talks about what the Leader of the Liberal Party did as Minister of Finance. The senior citizens of Canada will be very surprised to hear that the New Democratic Party does not support the indexation of senior citizens' pensions.
Who said anything about that?

The ultimate in hypocrisy is when the Member talks about corporate taxes and corporate write-offs. The absolute hypocritical flip-flop of the New Democratic Party on the flow-through shares issue is an indication of how phoney it is.
Why don't you answer the question?

shares was a corporate tax loophole which was supported not only by the Liberals, obviously not totally by the Conservatives since they have cut it back, but by the New Democratic Party.
The NDP House Leader was wearing a button in the House supporting this corporate loophole. So could the Member explain to me which loopholes he is in favour of now and which ones he is against? Madam Speaker, it was with interest I heard the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) expounding on the virtues of the Liberal Party and its history when it comes to tax reform. One Liberal attempt at tax reform in response to the Carter report was quite quickly shot down. I must say in all honesty that I think it was shot down because the Conservatives at that time, representing the vested interests, led quite a concerted attack against Carter's proposals, and the Government did back down.
Then we had the 10-year period when the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) was Minister of Finance in the Liberal Government. In fact, there was quite a turn-around in government policy during the rest of the 1970s. Many of the tax loopholes which now exist in the Income Tax Act, particularly those affecting the large corporations, were introduced at that time.
The Hon. Member for Hamilton East asked us what sort of loopholes we would close. I could mention to her that we would certainly have closed the loopholes that existed in 1982 which allowed the Royal Bank of Canada-and it was not the only one-to rack up some $360 million in profits and not pay one cent of tax, in fact, receive a tax credit of some $20 million. A woman working as a teller for the Royal Bank in 1982 would have actually paid more in taxes than the Royal Bank of Canada. That was in 1982. It was a result of the Liberal tax policies which allowed the Royal Bank to make a profit of over $360 million and not pay one cent of tax.
We would have closed down or never introduced the type of loophole that the Hon. Marc Lalonde introduced in 1983 to encourage research and development. That resulted in a loss of public revenues of close to $2.5 billion in less than six or seven months. That loophole became such a sham that when the Tories came to power, they recognized the type of abuse that

May 26, 1988
Excise Tax Act
was occurring and attempted to shut it down in October of 1984. However, in shutting it down they left the door open for those schemes that had been thought out, and so they introduced a grandfathering clause, and about one-third of the $2.5 billion lost in public revenues were lost in the period of time the Tories were in government.
Finally, the Tories themselves recognized they had not shut down this loophole tight enough, and in May of 1985 they shut it down completely. Of course, they should have done that in October of 1984 and would have saved the public Treasury well over $1 billion. That is the history of tax reform in this country. Unfortunately, we have never had proper tax reform. We have never accepted the notion that a buck is a buck, which was presented by the Carter Commission on Tax Reform. We continue to see inequities in the tax system which allow large and very profitable corporations not to pay any income tax whatsoever. We see inequities that allow high income wage earners in Canada to pay little, if any, tax, and inequities that see middle and lower income wage earners increasingly carrying the tax burden. That is true whether under a Liberal Government or under a Conservative Government.
The tax burden has increasingly fallen on middle and low-Canadian income earners. I think it is fair to say that in the 1950s, roughly half of public revenues came from the corporate side and half came from the individual taxpayers. Now, through successive Liberal and Conservative Governments, we find the proportion roughly to be 20 per cent, 25 per cent being paid by the corporate sector and some 75 per cent or 80 per cent being paid by individual Canadian taxpayers. That is the imbalance that has occurred over the years. Certainly, when we deal with the present legislation, Bill C-l 17, we can see it is just one more step in the road to extending the tax burden on ordinary Canadians.
This Bill brings together various budget proposals we have had placed in front of us in the last number of years. In fact, it seems that every time the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) stands up to make an economic statement, present a White Paper or introduce a Budget, there is invariably an increase in sales tax. Either the base is broadened, meaning that new items are now being taxed, or the rate has increased.
We can go down the list of all the various items the Government has introduced which increases the tax load on ordinary Canadians. There are such items as the 10 per cent tax on long-distance telephone calls and on paid television services. This will net the Government some $870 million a year. There is a sales tax on paint and wallpaper products, which has increased from 8 per cent to 12 per cent. It is estimated that this will bring the Government in an extra $60 million a year. Then there are taxes on beer, spirits, wine and tobacco products, which were previously announced, but not all in this Bill, which will bring the Government some extra revenue of $240 million a year.
One of the major increases the Minister of Finance, particularly, this Government, seems to like, is to increase the sales tax on gasoline. Since the Government has been in power it has raised the price of gasoline by some 23 cents a gallon. That is over and above what the Canadian taxpayers were paying before the Conservatives were elected. That is 23 cents a gallon extra going to the Federal Treasury.
We can discuss at some length the merits of the sales tax as opposed to other ways of gathering government revenues. I am certain there will be differences of opinion among all Members of the House as to whether the Government should raise its revenues more directly through the income tax and the corporate tax or whether it should do it through things like the sales tax. There are arguments in favour of having a sales tax. Most industrialized countries in fact do have a sales tax. It ensures that those individuals who pay little, if any, income tax, and I am referring to those higher income Canadians, at least pay some tax. In other words, the tax man stands in front of your pocket as the money leaves your pocket rather than as in the case of income tax which is taken before the money comes into your pocket.
Certainly, having a sales tax ensures that all those who spend money will be paying some tax. There are, of course, arguments against the sales tax. One of the major arguments is that it is regressive. That means that we are being taxed not on our ability to pay tax but on our needs. A person who has an income of $8,000, $10,000, $12,000 or $15,000 a year still needs to buy a gallon of milk and a loaf of bread. He must use the telephone. Perhaps he has a television set and is hooked into a cable company. He has to buy shoes and clothes for his kids. He has to buy a house or rent an apartment. He has to have a car. On all these items there will be, in some form or another, sales tax. He or she is being taxed at the same rate as the person who has an income of $100,000 or $1 million. Of course, those earning $100,000 or $1 million will be spending more and therefore will be paying more tax. However, on the basic necessities very often the low-income Canadian person will be paying the same amount of tax as the higher income Canadian person. That is not fair. It is regressive. It is one of the aspects of the sales tax that I find unacceptable.
The Government has said, and points out with some pride, that it has introduced the sales tax credit. It is supposed to compensate those with low incomes the money they have spent on sales taxes. But of course the sales tax credit is nowhere near what people are paying in sales taxes. The sales tax credit introduced by the Government does not touch the increases in the sales taxes that people will be paying because of various Tory Budgets. As with most other Canadians, they are paying more in tax but they are getting a little bit of it back now.
As well, the Government has failed to make a commitment that the sales tax credit will be indexed to inflation. That is something that the Government has to do as it increases its revenues from sales taxes. It has to guarantee to lower and
May 26, 1988

middle-income Canadians that as the sales tax increases, either through increasing the rate, the base or through inflation, low-income and middle-income Canadians will not be hurt any more, and that the sales tax credit will be indexed to ensure that they will get back the increases in taxes that they will be paying. Unfortunately, the Government has failed to move in that area.
There are some thorny issues dealing with sales tax in Canada. We have one of the most antiquated sales tax regimes in the world. I think everyone will admit that the present system is not a good one. I will now outline some of the various problems that we have.
One area with which we have difficulty in terms of the present sales tax regime concerns the difference in sales tax burden. The federal sales tax is levied on the manufacturers' selling price. However, the selling price may vary for the same product depending on whether the manufacturer sells it to a wholesaler or to a retailer. Selling to a retailer brings to it a higher relative tax burden. When a manufacturer sells his or her product to a retail outlet, higher costs will be incurred than if the product were sold to the retailer. In other words, what the present sales tax system does is to create distortions within the market-place. Therefore, some manufacturers who have set up their operations to sell directly to retailers will be paying one level of taxes, or taxes on a certain number of activities, whereas in another system of operating the business where the manufacturer sells to the wholesaler and the wholesaler sells to the retailer, one saves a significant amount on taxes.
In 1977, it was estimated that fully 44 per cent of taxable manufacturers' sales were directly to retailers. To reduce this discrimination there is now an extensive list of what are called notionable values which are used to discount the price at which a manufacturer sells a product to the retailer to the price that would have been paid by the wholesaler. But introducing notional value creates a lot of distortions within the system. The Federal Court has found that using notional value is discriminatory. It means that the Department of Revenue is able to place notional value on some goods. It is arbitrary. The court has found this to be unconstitutional. I would tend to say rightly so. That is one of the problems that we have with the present sales tax regime.
The other problem that we have is that the Government taxes the production of goods. In other words, those who produce capital goods have to pay the sales tax. There is no other country in the world that really taxes its capital goods. When purchasing intermediate goods to be used in the production process, the manufacturer inevitably ends up paying hidden sales taxes on some goods. It was estimated recently that 42 per cent of federal tax revenues were collected on intermediate and capital goods. What is particularly harmful about this is that in those industries that export their goods part of the export price includes the sales tax on the capital costs. No other country in the world puts a sales tax
Excise Tax Act
either directly or indirectly on the goods that they manufacture for export. But in good old Canada we do. There is something quite dumb about this.
Another area with which we have difficulty in our present sales tax regime is that it gives an advantage to importers. In other words, while we are taxing our exporters, we are giving advantages to importers. Canada does not include the cost of transporting goods to Canada as part of the cost base for the calculation of federal sales tax. Consequently, those imports competing with domestically produced goods often pay less tax than goods produced in Canada. Again, it does not really make much sense.
Another area with which we have concern is with respect to the complexity of the sales taxes. The licensing requirements on manufacturers and the documentation that this entails, the special exemptions for certain goods, the system of notional values, all tend to make the federal sales tax administratively very burdensome and unnecessarily complex. As a member of the Finance Committee I can say that we have been dealing with the Government's attempt to fix the present tax regime and some of the anomalies in it. There is a recognition on the part of the Government that taxing our exporters and giving advantage to the importers is something that the Government has to deal with.
As we have been going through the proposals and meeting with the manufacturers and the producers of many goods and services, we hear over and over again that what the Government is producing is even further complexity. As well, it is making the unfairness even more so. The difference between the imports and the exports and the unfairness there will be extended further with the proposed legislation that the Government is introducing. Again, it seems clear to us that the Government has no precise notion of what it wants to do with some of the inequities and some of the problems that exist in the sales tax regime.
One can go on as well about the extent to which the Government has relied upon the sales tax. As I mentioned before, the sale tax is essentially a regressive tax. It is unfair to low-income Canadians. However, it is also unfair to people living in remote communities. In fact, I would say it is unfair to those in all rural communities.
I see that the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) is in the House. He represents a district of many small rural communities. He surely must be concerned on their behalf at the type of increases in the sales tax. For example, there is the 10 per cent tax on communications. He knows and I know that when those people use their telephone it is often for a long-distance call.
I note that you are indicating to me, Madam Speaker, that my time is up. I wonder if I could just complete my thought on this and then there might be some questions that Hon. Members might wish to pose.

May 26, 1988
Excise Tax Act
The point I want to make is that all of us who represent wholly or in part rural districts must be concerned with increasing sales taxes because they have such a negative effect on rural communities. People in rural communities use longdistance telephone calls much more than city dwellers. A doctor may be in the next town. A cousin, mother or aunt perhaps lives down the highway and to call him or her requires a long-distance telephone call. People in rural communities are being taxed, not city dwellers.
The increase in the cost of gasoline means that if one is driving to the next town, more gasoline is being used. The cost of bringing in foodstuffs to the local store will be higher because of the increase in the gasoline prices that a trucker will have to pay. Sales taxes discriminate against those people living in rural and in remote communities.
Therefore, I urge those Conservative Members who represent districts with many rural areas to oppose this legislation.

In his remarks, the Hon. Member spent a good deal of time dealing with the unfairness of sales tax. I am aware, and I know the Hon. Member is aware that socialist Governments representing the same philosophy as the NDP, for example, the Government in New Zealand, imposed a sales tax on food and groceries. In Sweden, the socialist Government with the same philosophy as the NDP also imposed a sales tax on groceries and food products. I am not aware of the rate of tax in New Zealand, but I am aware that there are different rates of sales tax in Sweden, and that groceries are taxed at the highest rate.
In the event that the Hon. Member and his Party ever formed a Government, or if he and his Party had the balance of power in a minority government, would the NDP Members in Canada, like their colleagues whom they support regularly in Sweden and New Zealand, impose a sales tax on food?

That is a fair and honest question. I was with the Finance Committee when we visited New Zealand, and saw the operation of its sales tax. When the Labour Government in New Zealand introduced tax reform, it did it quite differently than tax reform in Canada. First, changes were introduced to the sales tax, to the income tax, and to the corporate tax. That Government also increased its subsidies or programs to help middle and low-income families. This was done at the same time, as opposed to what the Minister of Finance is doing and stretching it out.
When socialist democratic governments throughout the world introduce a sales tax on all goods and services, they guarantee that low and middle-income citizens are fully compensated. One might make a theoretical argument in favour of having a universal sales tax, but that can only be done when there is a full guarantee that low and middle-income citizens are fully compensated. For that, citizens have
to be able to trust their government to do that. The problem that I have is that I do not trust the Government.
After promising senior citizens that they would not have their pensions deindexed, the Government attempted to deindex their pensions. The Government deindexed family allowances and many social support systems. If there is not full indexation on the sales tax credit, then low-income Canadians will eventually lose. There can be a sales tax credit to fully compensate them this year, but if it is not fully indexed, next year it would be a little less, and the year after that a little less.
In part, Madam Speaker, it is a question of trust. Do you trust the Government to index fully the compensation that low-income people will receive? I do not trust the Government to do that. Therefore, I would be opposed to the Government imposing a tax on food and other basic necessities.

speechtext:
SUGGESTED REPEAL OF SECTION 17 Mr. Alan Redway (York East) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of repealing Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act and require that all remissions of taxes, fees or penalties be submitted, each year, to Parliament for approval.
He said: Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity of speaking in support of this motion which you have read calling upon the House to consider the advisability of asking the Government to repeal Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act, and to require that all remissions of taxes, fees or penalties be submitted to Parliament for approval each year.
The basic principle underlying all tax law is that it will apply equally and fairly to all Canadians regardless of who they are, where they live, or who they know; whether they be rich or poor, whether they be famous or notorious. The basic principle is that these laws should apply to everyone equally and absolutely. I would hope that that principle means, and I believe that it does, that each tax law will apply the same way to my neighbour next door, my neighbour across the street, or my neighbour in another part of the country in the same manner as it applies to me, and that I can expect that there will not be any favouritism offered to one person or another person.
That begs the question in my mind, and I hope in the minds of everyone in this House, as to whether the tax laws in Canada not only are supposed to apply that way equally to all but they actually do. In that respect I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that you should take a close look at Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act of Canada. That Act has a number of provisions which cause me concern. I would suspect it would cause you, other Members of this House and all Canadians concern.
Section 17(1) of the Financial Administration Act states:
The Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Treasury Board, whenever he considers it in the public interest, may remit any tax, fee or penalty.
That means he can forgive it, he can make a gift of it, he can make sure that it is not paid, that is if he considers it in the public interest. I am not certain as to how this process actually works in Parliament. I would assume that if a member of the bureaucracy draws up a list and provides on that list all of the people who are taxpayers who should have their taxes wiped out, then that list is submitted to the Governor in Council and the Governor in Council puts a stamp of approval on it and it is done. I do not know who is on that list particularly, Mr. Speaker. I do not know whether you know who is on that list, but apparently from time to time each year and every year the
Financial Administration Act
Governor in Council, through some process like that, forgives some people their taxes. Of course, other people in exactly the same circumstances may actually still be having to pay taxes. I would not suggest that it happens that way. There is the availability and there is the possibility in Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act for that sort of abuse, the kind of abuse where somehow or another, as a result of who you know or what you know, you may have your taxes forgiven and I may not, even though we are in the same circumstances or, for that matter, I may have my taxes forgiven and you may not, Mr. Speaker. I think this is a matter of serious concern and should be to you and all Canadians.
Subsection (3) of Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act goes into some detail as to how the Governor in Council can go through this forgiveness of taxes, or remission of taxes as it is called. It talks about not proceeding with a suit to recover those taxes. The Governor in Council might levy the tax but then decide not to pursue the recovery of it. He could delay or discontinue any proceedings to recover those taxes that are already commenced on the part of the Government. He could not enforce, or abandon any effort to collect those taxes, which is another provision in Section 17. Another one is to just write in the books that the tax has been paid, that it has been satisfied and that there is nothing owing on that particular tax. Another provision is to pay back money that is already paid. If somebody paid his taxes to the Government, to the Receiver General, there is the right in Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act to take the money and send it back saying "Thanks anyway. We don't need your money. Forget about it. We are sending it back". This is the sort of thing that Section 17 provides for.
I wonder how many people in this House and across Canada realize that there is in Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act, the authority to forgive somebody's taxes and not have to seek the approval of Parliament first in order to do it. In other words, Parliament has already given the Governor in Council that authority not to do it once in a particular case but to do it time and time again, day after day, month after month, year after year. That is what Section 17 has the effect of doing.
Does the Government ever act on this authority in Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act? It certainly does. But it has been very difficult to know about the action which the Government has been taking. You may know, Mr. Speaker, that every year in the fall the Government publishes something called the Public Accounts of Canada. It comes out not as a single volume book but it is in four separate volumes at the moment. I suppose that as the complexity grows there may be five and six volumes, whatever number, but it is a lot of paper. I am not sure how many people ever sit down and read through it all.
I tried to find the material on tax remissions in the Public Accounts of Canada a few months ago and had to seek assistance from the Library of Parliament because I could not find it in the Public Accounts when I looked. The reason I

May 26, 1988
Financial Administration Act
could not find it is that it is in Volume II, Part 2 of the Public Accounts of Canada under something called Additional Information and Analysis. Section 3 in the middle says "Supplementary Information Required by the Financial Administration Act". Section 3 is 36 pages of tax remissions or tax forgiveness of one sort or another. It is 36 pages of the Public Accounts of Canada hidden under the title Supplementary Information Required by the Financial Administration Act.
You would not only have to get a Philadelphia lawyer or a parliamentary expert, you would have to be the Auditor General to figure out where this information is in the Public Accounts of Canada. There are 36 pages in the last Public Accounts which were for the fiscal year 1986-87. Another financial year has gone by now and we do not know how many taxes have been given away under Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act since that time. But in the 1986-87 fiscal year there was almost $ 1 billion worth of taxes remitted under the authority of sections like Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act. An amount of $914,278,119 was given away, tax money that was levied under the tax laws of Canada. Everybody is supposed to be treated equally under those laws, but $1 billion was given back to people who were supposed to be paying taxes under those provisions. That is just for the fiscal year 1986-87.
Back in 1986, the Public Accounts Committee of this House took a look at one particular tax remission. It dealt with Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited and Dome Petroleum Limited. It was found that a remission order had been issued pursuant to Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act in February, 1985, to Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas, a subsidiary of Dome Petroleum Limited. Over a 10-year period Hudson's Bay was authorized to deduct for income tax purposes the financing costs that Dome incurred in acquiring it. This is actually the cost of one company acquiring another. This was forgiven under one of these provisions of Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act. The value of that remission order was considered and estimated at the date of this report back in 1986 at some $400 million. This $400 million was given back under the provisions of Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act. Parliament's permission was not required.
These tax laws would have applied the same way to other companies, but other companies would not have got a tax gift of $400 million. Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company, however, got this tax benefit. This expenditure never came to Parliament for consideration or approval whatsoever.
In the report of the Public Accounts Committee dealing with that one tax remission, the Public Accounts Committee suggested that the Government should give consideration to amending the Financial Administration Act to require: first, the tabling in Parliament of all income tax remission orders; second, the preparation of an explanatory note to accompany
each remission order so tabled outlining why the remission order is in the public interest; third, the reference of all remission orders so tabled to the appropriate Standing Committee; and finally, the prior approval by Parliament of all income tax remission orders exceeding $20 million in value.
The thrust of my motion is not just that tax remissions exceeding $20 million should be approved by Parliament, but in fact that all tax remissions should be approved by Parliament. I am not suggesting that we should spend the entire parliamentary year debating tax remissions. It may be that the vast majority of them, and maybe all of them, flow from rational and understandable decisions on the part of the Government. If the facts were placed before the House, perhaps we would all agree to them without question.
My suggestion is merely that we devote some limited time of the House to allow a little debate each year and to actually pass an approval motion so that it just does not happen behind curtains, behind closed doors or under the veil of secrecy where the Privacy Act and the Access to Information Act do not apply. We should be getting these things right out on the floor, making sure that we understand and know why these tax remissions are taking place, and not only those for $20 million but all tax remissions. If it makes sense, sure, we will approve them in short order, and that will be the end of it.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) responded to the report of the Public Accounts Committee in a letter addressed to the Chairman of the committee on March 9, 1987. I would like to quote certain portions of the letter. The Minister of Finance wrote:
Before dealing in turn with the specific recommendations in the report I should note that I share some of the committee's concerns respecting the remission order process. My responses to some of your recommendations reflect my commitment to improving the process.
The Minister of Finance went on to say:
As you know most remission orders are currently published in the Canada Gazette within 23 days from their passage by the Governor in Council.
In response to your recommendation that all income tax remission orders be tabled in Parliament, I propose that they all be published in the Canada Gazette and that the orders above a $20 million threshold be tabled in Parliament on a regular and timely basis. Secondly, I propose to present to Parliament periodic reports of all remission orders. These periodic reports will contain all information that is currently available in the annual public accounts reports, namely the registration number, date, nature and amount of remission (where an amount is available).
These reports would also contain information that is not currently required for public accounts purposes. In keeping with your recommendation 7b and 17, the proposed reports would include an explanatory note setting out the reasons for the order and, where an amount is not specified in the order, an estimate of the amount to be remitted where an estimate is practicable.
Your Committee's principal recommendation is that all income tax remission orders should be approved by Parliament.
That was not really the thrust of the recommendation. It was only that those over $20 million be approved. The thrust of my motion, however, is that all of them be approved by Parliament. The Minister went on to say:
May 26, 1988

While I recognize that Parliament needs to be fully informed with respect to remission orders, I believe that the power to grant remission orders was given to government for valid reasons that continue to exist. Indeed, it is desirable to maintain the capacity to respond swiftly, effectively and unequivocally where it is necessary to rectify anomalies, unintended results and injustices in the tax system. To require Parliamentary approval of all or some remission orders could seriously impair the effectiveness and timeliness of remission orders and would limit considerably the flexibility of our tax system.
The Minister went on to say:
One recent example was the remission order granting withholding tax relief for interest on government and long-term corporate debt pending the necessary changes in tax law. Thus, my response to this recommendation is the same as my response of the Eighth Report of the Joint Standing Committee on regulations and other statutory instruments concerning the use of general remission orders. That is, while I have and will continue to avoid the use of remission orders to implement government policy I believe that such orders are an appropriate method for the government to use to grant timely relief.
In effect, the Minister said two things. He said first that he thinks Parliament should have more information about these tax gifts, but he said as well that he does not think that Parliament should have the right to approve them because it is more expeditious for the Government to deal with them.
In fairness to the Minister, just a few days ago, I received a report to Parliament on remission orders approved in the six-month period ending March 31, 1988, and that indicates that it is in response to the recommendations of the Public Accounts Committee in connection with remission orders. It indicates as well that the Minister has decided to table semiannual reports in Parliament on these tax gifts and that such reports will be for a six-month period ending March 31 and September 30 each year. We will get one of these reports and it will set out some explanations about what it is all about and how much the tax gifts have been and that sort of thing.
In fairness to the Minister, he has proceeded with that, but in my view, the Minister misses the point, which is, that it is not necessarily necessary to curtail the authority of the Government to make tax remissions for these wonderful purposes that he outlines here, including correcting anomalies and injustices. It is not necessary to curtail that, but surely it should be necessary for us as a Parliament to approve them, to have this information before us and to be able to ask questions about whether or not everyone is being treated fairly, and to be assured that they are before we actually approve them and enshrine them, whether retroactively or before the fact.
One of the things that bothers me is something that was reported in today's Globe and Mail. One of our colleagues, the Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Boyer), raised the question of tax remissions to the Goodyear Tire and Rubber Co. There was a report in The Globe and Mail today, as reported in Quorum, dealing with this issue. Part of the end of the article reads:
Gerald Wright, senior policy adviser to Mr. Hockin, said it has not been decided whether Ottawa will help Goodyear Canada. Any federal aid would be extended through a duty remission program for tire manufacturers.
That certainly was not the purpose of Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act, but that in effect is what it is being used for. Surely Parliament should have the right to
Financial Administration Act
approve these tax gifts and giveaways to ensure that every Canadian is being treated exactly the same way and to provide that because of something that goes on behind closed doors, one may not be getting a break that no one else gets.
1 hope that the House will approve this motion and that we can get on with repealing Section 17 and getting Financial control back in the hands of Parliament and out of the hands of the bureaucracy.

There is in mine. The phrase about submitting "each year to Parliament for approval" means to me that it would have to be submitted for approval prior to the remission actually taking place. If that were not the case, it would not be approval per se.
If that is what the Hon. Member intends, I have some difficulty with it. Remission of penalties, fines, fees of all kinds sometimes has to be done simply because they were collected erroneously to start with. Of course, that is the reason that it is sometimes necessary to remit taxes, fees and penalties to the person who paid them in the first place.
The Hon. Member referred to these remissions as tax gifts to Canadians. That could very well be true in a number of cases. However, not all remissions are tax gifts. If an amount were erroneously collected, then it is not a gift, it is simply reimbursement.

I would however like to commend the Hon. Member for having brought to our attention this matter of some importance since it is obvious, as he has noted, that when these policies on tax remissions were established, when the House, by way of Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act, empowered government to make such tax remissions, it was not the legislator's intention to grant Government the power to use the back door to hand out grants. And this is indeed happening in certain cases.
My colleague has just given us a concrete example, that of Goodyear, where federal Government officials, speaking for the Minister of State (Finance), have indicated that if a grant was to be made, it would be made by way of tariff remissions.
In that case, Madam Speaker, I have to agree with the Hon. Member that when a remission is in fact used in lieu of a

Financial Administration Act
grant, then Parliament certainly has the right, and the duty as I see it, to have a say on the establishment of the program.

However, we should note that the Standing Committee on Public Accounts did not ask for exactly what the Hon. Member is suggesting today. I think he recognized that when he said a little earlier that he was going beyond the request made by that committee, of which he is a member.
The committee asked that all income tax remission orders be tabled in Parliament. It said nothing about remission orders other than those dealing with income tax. The committee asked also for a preparation of an explanatory note to accompany each remission order in order to explain to legislators why the amount was remitted to start with. That is entirely reasonable. The committee also requested that there be a reference of all remission orders tabled in that way. In other words, the remission orders relating to income tax would be referred to the standing committee. That did not apply to duties or penalties or anything else, just those related to income tax.
As well, the committee asked that there be prior approval by Parliament of income tax remission orders exceeding $20 million. In other words, with respect to amounts less than $20 million, the remission orders would be tabled in the House, but not to obtain approval. We could review them as we review Order in Council appointments, perhaps. However, the House would have a say on whether or not amounts in excess of $20 million would be remitted. That is far narrower, as I understand it, than what the Hon. Member has suggested today.
When the committee made this recommendation to the Government, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) replied that the committee's principal recommendation is that all income tax remission orders should be approved by Parliament. Obviously he misunderstood what was in the committee's report. The committee said it wanted all income tax remission orders to be tabled in Parliament, but that only those involving amounts greater than $20 million would require approval. I do not think the Minister's reply was adequate, but that was so because he did not seem to have understood what the committee was asking. In any case, the Minister made his response and concluded with several remarks to the Chairman of the committee. Basically we are not very much further ahead than that today, except that certain documents are now being tabled in the House.
We have a request made by a committee of Parliament which was misunderstood by the Minister. He of course then arrived at the wrong conclusion. On the other hand, we have a Member asking that we go well beyond what the committee requested and that we seek parliamentary approval of all remission orders.
There are questions that beg to be asked. I do not know whether it was the intent of the Member to go this far, probably not, but I pose the following question. Under the
