speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to respond to the proposal in this motion to change the existing procedure for granting remissions of taxes and tariffs.
Madam Speaker, I think it is fair to say that there is a rather low level of public understanding of the workings of the tax and tariff remission system. Therefore I hope that this debate can shed some light on the subject and focus attention on the important issues that are involved, and that my colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) will be able to follow the debate and fully appreciate the nature of the problem.
As the House is aware, the Standing Committee on Public Accounts has concerned itself with the question of tax and tariff remissions. The Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway), sponsor of the motion before the House, has taken an active role in the committee's discussions. Madam Speaker, the motion deals with one of the issues that were discussed in the committee-that of the approval process for granting remissions. But the committee was also very much concerned with other remission issues, and notably the need for greater accountability and openness by government in advising Parliament about remission orders that have been made. I would like to deal with that aspect of the matter in my opening remarks because of its importance.
The accountability of government to Parliament for its actions is of foremost concern to all of us. In the area of tax and tariff remissions, I submit that this Government has made a major advance in ensuring a high degree of openness and accountability for its actions. In March of last year, in response to concerns expressed by the Public Accounts
May 26, 1988

Committee, the Minister of Finance took three major commitments: first, to publish all income tax remission orders in the Gazette; second, to table all income tax remission orders involving more than $20 million; and third, to implement a new reporting process to Parliament covering all new remission orders.
In carrying out his undertaking, the Minister is taking steps even beyond those commitments. All remission orders, and not just those for income tax remissions, will be Gazetted. Similarly, the promise to table in Parliament orders involving more than $20 million will also apply to tariff remissions as well as those for income tax. These steps have already been implemented. The third step-to put in place a timely and practical process of reporting to Parliament all new remission orders-will be implemented in the very near future. This will involve a report after every six months on orders issued during that period. It will provide all of the information now given in the annual Public Accounts, and also set out the concise reasons for making the order and, where possible, the amount of tax or tariff being forgone or an estimate of the cost to the Treasury.
These measures will be a large improvement on the former practice. Most orders have in the past been listed in the Gazette although some were not-those affecting an individual or orders not of a continuing nature. Now all orders will be published. Moreover, publication in the Gazette did not provide very easy accessibility to Members. Nor did it provide important information that Members should know. The new system demonstrates the real concern of the Minister of Finance in bringing greater transparency to the remission process and creating the basis for real accountability by governement for its actions in this area.
Madam Speaker, I should add that this new reporting system is only part of a much broader approach by the Minister to opening up the process of budget making and tax reform. In his first budget in 1985 the Minister issued a paper setting out proposals for improving the budget process. That process has involved very broad consultation with the public on potential new tax measures prior to every budget since then. The consultation process showed its value particularly in developing the important measures of tax reform which were announced last year. The widest possible range of interested individuals, groups and associations were consulted and had an opportunity to make their views known. The Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs also made important contributions in the process of consultation.
So what is being done in relation to tax and tariff remission orders is in keeping with the government's overall approach to greater openness and accountability.
The Public Accounts Committee and the Auditor-General were also concerned about the need for evaluating remission orders and ensuring that they do in fact achieve their purposes. Here too the Government has taken action. A new Tax
Financial Administration Act
Measures Evaluation Division has been set up in the Department of Finance. Its purpose is to evaluate not only tax measures but also the more significant tax and tariff remission programs. This new division was itself a response to one of the concerns of the Public Accounts Committee.
So it is very clear, Madam Speaker, that the Minister of Finance shares many of the concerns of the Public Accounts Committee and has been responsive to them. He has not, however, supported the kind of approach proposed in the motion by the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway). There are good and valid reasons for the position taken by the Minister.
First, however, I should comment on the specific proposal that is embodied in this motion. It would do away with the remission process provided under section 17 of the Financial Administration Act. In its place, it proposes an annual submission to Parliament, for its approval, of all requests for remissions of taxes, fees or penalties.
I should note that the Financial Administration Act remission system applies only to tax remissions. Since January, tariff remissions have been provided under the Customs Tariff and thus would be outside the scope of this motion. The House should know that about 95 per cent of the amount of all remissions involve tariffs.
In considering this motion, however, the important point is whether it would serve the public interest. I submit that it would not, Madam Speaker. And one has only to look at the nature of the great majority of remission orders to realize that a system that requires prior Parliamentary approval would be quite inappropriate.
The large majority of remission orders, for either income tax or tariffs, are granted for reasons of equity-cases, for example, where there has been over-payment of taxes and duties and the letter of the law does not permit a refund or other relief. There are plenty of examples in the remission orders that have been made public. Cases like that of a mother with a claim for $654 in tax refund in respect of child tax credits for 1979. Because she had not filed her claim within the deadline required by law, as you would know, Madam Speaker, there was no way legally to pay the refundable child tax credit which she very much needed. The only recourse was through a remission order.
Another example involved a fairly new product on the market-beer coolers-and the Government decision to remit the excise tax payable on wine that is blended with beer in a brewery. Without that remission there would have been double taxation: the excise tax paid on wine purchased by the brewery to make its beer cooler, and a further excise duty paid on the end product shipped from the brewery. A remission order was the only, the quickest and most direct way of correcting this inequity created by the advent of a new product. The brewery needed relief from a double tax situation that could not have been foreseen when the excise tax and duty legislation was

May 26, 1988
Financial Administration Act
written. Of course, the legislation could be amended, and this no doubt will be done if the situation persists.
But as Members know, changing legislation is a timeconsuming and costly process. And in the meantime it could not help the brewer who wants to develop a market for this product now, not in six months or a year.
This requirement for prompt relieving action is a common thread running through most remission cases. The Public Accounts Committee has also been concerned that relief in remission cases should not be delayed.
The Government's position was well summarized by the Minister of Finance in a letter dated March 8, 1987 to the Public Accounts Committee in response to a committee report. Allow me to quote from that letter: "While I recognize that Parliament needs to be fully informed with respect to remission orders, I believe that the power to grant remission orders was given to government for valid reasons that continue to exist. Indeed it is desirable to maintain the capacity to respond swiftly, effectively and unequivocally where it is necessary to rectify anomalies, unintended results and injustices in the tax system. To require parliamentary approval of all or some remission orders could seriously impair the effectiveness and timeliness of remission orders and would limit considerably the flexibility of our tax system."
Madam Speaker, the Minister was referring to the great majority of remission cases which involve situations of inequity, hardships and injustices. And I am convinced, Madam Speaker, that my colleague from Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) would not condone unfair taxation.

In addition, as Members know-and I hope they know, Madam Speaker-there are a relatively small number of tariff remission cases, usually involving quite substantial amount, which are more in the nature of industrial programs. They are usually conditional on the industry carrying out specific undertakings or performances such as major investments.
Under the tax system, such cases will be reported promptly to Parliament. And like any government action they will be open to questioning and challenge. That is the essence of government accountability, which is fully supported by the Minister. This Government will not be making any remission orders that it is not fully prepared to explain and defend in Parliament.
Members should be aware, however, that the number of such so-called duty remission programs will substantially decline. That is because of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. The Agreement specifically provides that no new or expanded tariff relief provisions which include performance requirements by an industry shall be introduced after next June 30 or after congressional approval of the agreement. Such remission programs that are now in effect are to be
terminated before the end of the 10-year term of the agreement January 1, 1998.
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, I submit that we should not adopt the major change to our remission system proposed in the motion before us. The present system is a good and workable one, improved as it has been with the recent changes ensuring much greater openness and answerability to Parliament by the Government for its remission orders.

Madam Speaker, I am glad the Member for York East (Mr. Redway) has raised this particular issue. While I have reservations about the specifics of his proposal, his effort to bring greater openness, open government, and accountability on the question of tax remissions is very desirable.
I respect the kind of quixotic way in which he continues within the Conservative Party to carry on this campaign. However, after three and a half years in the House, I think he should have realized that the Conservative Party, like the Liberals before it, is beyond repair, and he should either join his colleagues on the independent benches on this side or come over to the New Democratic Party.
I believe the whole question of openness is fundamental to many Canadians in terms of their sense of whether or not the tax system is really fair. The Hon. Member for York East cited the case of Dome and the remission order of Hudson's Bay Gas which involved the forgiveness of some $400 million.
The Government is saying that in the future, remissions that have a value exceeding $20 million will be reported in some way or another to the House of Commons. I suppose that represents some progress. I am unaware of the mechanism to be established and, as finance spokesperson for my Party, I have yet to see any of these reports about how taxpayers' money is being spent through remissions under Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act.
There are several questions with which we must deal. For example, should Section 17 be repealed? Section 17 is exceedingly broad. I will read a couple of paragraphs into the record. Section 17(1) states:
The Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Treasury Board, whenever he considers it in the public interest, may remit any tax, fee or penalty.
For example, if the Cabinet decrees that returning all the income tax to people who are registered members of the Rhinoceros Party or other political Party is in the public interest, it can do so. While there may be some criticism from the public, it has that power.
Those orders are rather frequently gazetted in the The Canada Gazette which is a publication of mind-stupefying complexity and opacity. It is very difficult to understand in order to know what is happening.

The Canada Gazette in February, 1988, contained a lengthy amendment order under Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act, dealing with commercial vehicles. It is apparently justified because of the need to ensure consistency with the new customs tariff. Perhaps there is no specific value to that because the new order has the same value as the old order. However, the point is that, apart from gazetting, the House of Commons was not consulted or informed.
On the other hand, in 1973 and 1974, a number of trade union members on the Victoria Colonist were on strike and set up a union paper during the period of the strike which I believe was known as the Victoria Express. They were compelled to pay tax and, for various reasons which are not spelled out, the current Government decided to remit the tax that was either owing or had been paid by those trade union members. Patricia Turnbull is gazetted as receiving $1.14 for tax paid for the fiscal year 1973 and $40.60 for 1974.
I believe the Hon. Member for York East would agree that a few tens of thousands of dollars in taxes remitted in this particular case is somewhat small for the House of Commons to deal with by means of a vote or legislation. On the other hand, I think he would also agree that stating that only those remissions worth more than $20 million would be studied is a little too large an amount.
For example, I do not know the value of the remission cited by the Parliamentary Secretary, which he said was to avoid double taxing, where wines are used for wine coolers and are mixed in various ways with beer. That is something I would welcome right now. That is not a relevant comment, but it may be appropriate at the end of the day.

Financial Administration Act
Should Parliament have the right to review major remissions? In my opinion, the answer is yes. I believe we must go beyond that and look at the whole question of tax expenditures, which include these remissions and far beyond.
The Auditor General pointed out in his 1984 report that the federal Government now spends about 30 cents to 50 cents through the tax system for every $1 of government spending. The Nielsen Task Force in 1983 estimated that 1983 tax expenditures totalled $36 billion compared to direct expenditures of $57 billion. So if we are now getting a report every six months from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) of the value of all remission orders, that is just a very small start to the kind of openness I believe we should be looking at.
In the minority report which my colleague from Regina and I submitted on the question of tax reform, we urged that every tax expenditure should be reviewed first by the relevant Department, so it could be looked at with respect to alternative policy instruments. Then there should be an appropriate tax expenditure analysis presented annually, along with the spending Estimates in the budget of the Public Accounts, and tax expenditures of all kinds-and we are talking about $40 billion or $50 billion a year-should be integrated with the spending envelope system and, therefore, subject to cabinet committee control. Finally, they should be subject to the approval of Parliament.
I note, and this is a sign of the kind of weakness of the system, that the Nielsen Task Force, which my Party criticized because of the way it handled this question of public spending, was looking at the trees and not at the forest and in fact spent a total of about 3 per cent or 4 per cent of the number of pages they produced in commenting on government expenditures, commenting on tax expenditures, which amount to some 30 per cent or 40 per cent of tax expenditures. It would certainly amount to far more than that when one looks at program expenditures.
While I have questions about eliminating Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act, I believe that the thrust of the argument of my friend from York East is an appropriate one. If he will join with us in bringing about greater accountability and openness, if he will go beyond this question of the remission orders under Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act to the whole question of tax expenditures in general, and if he will join us in trying to ensure that all tax expenditures are voted upon every year, then regardless of whether or not he joins the NDP caucus, I know on this issue we can work solidly and very positively together.

Madam Speaker, the Government welcomes this chance to consider remission orders in the context of the Bill presented by the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway). It has been, and continues to be, this Government's objective to increase openness and accountability in the tax and tariff system. Let us look first at the budget

May 26, 1988
Financial Administration Act
process. Members will know of the steps we have taken specifically to open up the budget process as far as possible and to have widespread consultation and examination of potential tax measures. In line with these objectives, in our very first Budget in 1985 we presented a paper entitled The Canadian Budget Process: Proposals for Improvement.
Our approach was also illustrated in the tax reform process. Before undertaking reforms, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) made himself and officials available to a large number of groups covering most social interest groups, the business community, volunteer organizations, economists, representatives of small and medium-sized businesses, unions and so on. After the proposals were published in the White Paper, the Minister again undertook to meet representatives from affected sectors who had things to say and representations to make.
Next, the proposals in the White Paper were examined in the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs, which was chaired by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), the committee on which I am happy to serve. This committee traversed the country and held hearings. Almost every imaginable group was heard from. The report of the committee contained 81 recommendations, to which the Minister of Finance in turn responded.
We have said that this process of tax reform has been one of the most open in the history of the federal Government. All affected individuals, taxpayers and citizens had several opportunities to speak with decision-makers. The process followed on tax reform also is a good example of how the Government's policy of widespread consultation interacts with the wider powers given to committees of this House.
With respect to remission orders, the Public Accounts Committee in its first report was extremely critical of the remission's process in an income tax order concerning the acquisition of Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas by Dome. This was an order passed by a previous Government. In responding to the committee on behalf of the Government, the Minister of Finance indicated that he also had concerns about accountability in the remission process. The Government immediately took steps to open up the process and make it more accountable. It specifically undertook to publish all income tax orders in The Gazette, to table in Parliament all income tax orders over $20 million, and to report periodically to Parliament on all new income tax remission orders and to give as much information as possible on their costs and rationale.
As my colleague, the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Dorin) reported to the House a few moments ago, one of these six month reports to Parliament on remission orders is available to all Members of Parliament. It was specifically in response to the recommendations of the Public Accounts Committee.
In the course of carrying out these commitments, it was realized that any report on income tax remissions would be a pretty slim report. A review by the Office of the Comptroller
General indicated that income tax orders, for instance, comprised less than 5 per cent of the value of all remission orders. It was also hard to see why other remission orders should not get the same open treatment as income tax orders. The Government, therefore, decided to table all remission orders worth $20 million or more in the House, to publish all remission orders in The Gazette and to issue a six-monthly report on all new remission orders to the House.
Let me say in conclusion on this point that the Government can claim credit for making the remission process more accountable, for promptly responding to concerns expressed about this process in a committee of this House and, indeed, for going much further than its original commitment to Parliament to make the remission process more accountable. Instead of just having an open process for income tax remission orders, all remission orders, including tariff, excise and sales tax orders, are now included in a more accountable process.
Placing the remission order process in a wider context, this is only one of the steps the Government has taken to increase accountability and openness in the tax and tariff system. Other steps include increased and wider consultation and the increased role of committees of the House.
It is important not only to be accountable but to be seen to be accountable. In the latter respect, the Government has also been increasing its efforts to make information on remissions accessible to Members. I have already remarked on some of these efforts such as the six-monthly report on new remission orders and the tabling in Parliament of all orders over $20 million. At the same time, efforts have been made to increase the usefulness of information in the annual Public Accounts.
For instance, these accounts will now give the annual amounts remitted under an order for the duration of its life. Some information will also be excluded to make the accounts more meaningful. Thus, a recent order remitted some $60,000 of tax paid on strike benefits to 298 members of a union. Previously, the Public Accounts would have listed all these individuals and the amounts they received. This information will still be available at Revenue Canada for any member of the public who wants to inquire about the order, but the Public Accounts will not list the individual beneficiaries of this order over several pages.
In conclusion, emphasis has also been put on increasing the meaningfulness of information in the Public Accounts without sacrificing public access to information.
